sections.title: 1. Equity Securities — Definition and Ownership Fundamentals
sections.overview: An equity security represents an ownership (residual) interest in a corporation. Equity holders are residual claimants with limited liability, meaning their loss is capped at the amount invested. Federal securities law defines the term broadly to include common and preferred stock, securities convertible into stock, warrants, rights, and similar instruments.
key_concepts: Equity = ownership; debt = creditor relationship.
Limited liability: shareholder loss capped at investment amount; personal assets are not at risk.

Order of liquidation (priority of claims): (1) secured creditors, (2) unsecured creditors/general creditors including debenture holders, (3) subordinated debt, (4) preferred stockholders, (5) common stockholders (residual).
Authorized shares vs. issued shares vs. outstanding shares vs. treasury stock (issued − outstanding = treasury).
Statutory definition of 'equity security' includes stock, treasury stock, securities convertible into stock, warrants, rights, and other interests commonly known as equity securities.
U.S.-listed equity trades (and ADRs) settle T+1 (per SEC settlement rule, effective May 28, 2024).
rules: 17 CFR 240.3a11-1 — defines 'equity security' under the Exchange Act to include stock, similar securities, convertibles, warrants, rights, and any interest commonly known as an equity security.
17 CFR 240.10b-18 — provides a safe harbor for issuer repurchases of its own common stock from manipulation liability when conditions on manner, timing, price, and volume are satisfied.
formulas: Outstanding shares = Issued shares − Treasury shares
Shareholders' Equity = Assets − Liabilities (per OpenStax Financial Accounting accounting equation)
mnemonics: Liquidation order: 'Some Unpaid Suits Prefer Common' — Secured, Unsecured, Subordinated, Preferred, Common.

sections.title: 2. Common Stock
sections.overview: Common stock confers ownership, voting rights, a residual claim on earnings and assets, and limited liability. Returns come from price appreciation and discretionary dividends declared by the board.
key_concepts: Voting rights: typically one vote per share on directors and major corporate matters (charter amendments, mergers, dissolution).
Statutory voting: one vote per share per director seat (favors majority holders).
Cumulative voting: shareholder may aggregate votes across seats (favors minority holders).
Preemptive right: existing shareholders may maintain proportional ownership in new share issuances (often delivered via a rights offering).
Residual claim on earnings (dividends are discretionary, not guaranteed) and on assets at liquidation (paid last).
Dividend mechanics: Declaration date → Ex-dividend date → Record date → Payable date. Under T+1 settlement, ex-date and record date generally coincide (ex-date = record date).
Stock split (forward) increases share count, reduces per-share price proportionally; reverse split does the opposite. Total market value and ownership percentage unchanged.
Treasury stock: repurchased shares; no voting rights, no dividends.
rules: 17 CFR 240.10b-18 — safe harbor for issuer common-stock buybacks.
formulas: EPS = (Net Income − Preferred Dividends) / Weighted Avg. Common Shares Outstanding
P/E Ratio = Market Price per Share / EPS
Dividend Yield = Annual Dividend per Share / Market Price per Share
Dividend Payout Ratio = Dividends per Share / EPS
Book Value per Common Share = (Common Equity − Preferred Equity) / Common Shares Outstanding
Cumulative voting max votes per candidate = Shares Owned × Number of Director Seats up
mnemonics: Dividend dates: 'DERP' — Declaration, Ex-date, Record, Payable.
Common stockholder rights: 'V-LIPS' — Vote, Limited liability, Inspect books, Preemptive (if granted), Sue (derivative).

sections.title: 3. Preferred Stock
sections.overview: Preferred stock is an equity security with a fixed stated dividend and seniority over common in dividends and liquidation but junior to all debt. It generally lacks voting rights and behaves like a fixed-income/interest-rate-sensitive instrument.
key_concepts: Stated par value (commonly $100) used to compute the fixed dividend (e.g., 6% preferred on $100 par = $6/yr).
Dividend payment is at board discretion but must be paid before any common dividend.
Generally non-voting; voting rights may activate if dividends are skipped (depends on charter).
Interest-rate sensitive: prices fall when rates rise (inverse relationship), similar to long-duration bonds.

Types: Straight (non-cumulative); Cumulative (missed dividends accrue as 'dividends in arrears' and must be paid before common); Participating (may receive extra above stated rate); Convertible (exchangeable into a fixed number of common shares); Callable (issuer may redeem at stated call price); Adjustable-rate (dividend resets to a benchmark).
Liquidation priority: senior to common, junior to all bondholders and general creditors.
rules: 17 CFR 240.3a11-1 — preferred stock falls within the definition of equity security.
formulas: Annual Preferred Dividend = Stated Rate × Par Value
Current Yield (preferred) = Annual Dividend / Market Price
Conversion Ratio = Par Value of Preferred / Conversion Price
Parity Price (common) = Market Price of Preferred / Conversion Ratio
mnemonics: Preferred features: 'CCPA' — Cumulative, Convertible, Participating, Adjustable (plus Callable).
Preferred ranks 'between debt and common' — senior to common in dividends and liquidation; junior to all debt.

sections.title: 4. Rights (Subscription Rights / Preemptive Rights Offerings)
sections.overview: A rights offering allows existing shareholders to purchase additional shares of a new issue at a discount, in proportion to current ownership, before the issue is offered publicly. Rights are short-term (typically 30–45 days) and may be exercised, sold, or allowed to expire.
key_concepts: Issued only to existing shareholders to satisfy preemptive rights and prevent ownership dilution.
One right typically issued per share owned; multiple rights plus cash required to subscribe to one new share.
Subscription price is below current market price (intrinsic value).
Short life span (~30–45 days); trade separately during subscription period.
Cum-rights vs. ex-rights pricing reflects whether the buyer is entitled to the rights.
Standby underwriting: investment bank agrees to purchase any unsubscribed shares.
Rights are typically registered under the Securities Act of 1933 unless exempt.
rules: 17 CFR 240.3a11-1 — rights are included within 'equity security'.
formulas: Value of a Right (cum-rights) = (Market Price − Subscription Price) / (Rights Needed + 1)
Value of a Right (ex-rights) = (Market Price − Subscription Price) / Rights Needed
Theoretical Ex-Rights Price = [(Old Price × Old Shares) + (Subscription Price × New Shares)] / Total Shares
mnemonics: Rights = 'Right now, Reduced price, Short-term, Shareholders only.'

sections.title: 5. Warrants
sections.overview: Warrants are long-term equity securities giving the holder the right (not obligation) to buy stock from the issuer at a fixed price. They are typically issued as 'sweeteners' attached to bond or preferred offerings to enhance marketability.
key_concepts: Issued by the corporation itself (not by an exchange or OCC) — exercising a warrant creates new shares (dilutive).
Long maturity (often 5–10 years; some perpetual).
Strike (exercise) price is set ABOVE the market price at issuance — no intrinsic value at issuance, only time value.
Often detachable from the host security and trade independently.
No voting rights, no dividends until exercised.
Compare to rights: rights have short life and below-market subscription price; warrants have long life and above-market exercise price.
formulas: Intrinsic Value of Warrant = max(0, Market Price − Exercise Price)
Warrant Premium = Warrant Price − Intrinsic Value
mnemonics: Rights vs. Warrants: 'Rights are Right now (short, below market); Warrants Wait (long, above market).'

sections.title: 6. American Depositary Receipts (ADRs)
sections.overview: ADRs are negotiable certificates issued by a U.S. depositary bank representing ownership of a specified number of shares (or fractions) of a foreign company's stock held on deposit abroad. They allow U.S. investors to trade foreign equities in U.S. dollars on U.S. markets.
key_concepts: Issued by U.S. depositary banks; underlying foreign shares held by a custodian in the home country.
Quoted and traded in U.S. dollars; dividends paid in U.S. dollars (after currency conversion).
ADR holders typically have NO direct voting rights or preemptive rights; the depositary bank exercises voting per ADR program terms.
Risks: currency/exchange rate risk, political risk, foreign-tax withholding on dividends (may be eligible for U.S. foreign tax credit).
Sponsored ADR: foreign company contracts with one depositary bank (most listed ADRs). Unsponsored: multiple banks may issue without issuer involvement.
ADR levels: Level I (OTC), Level II (listed, no capital raised), Level III (listed, used to raise capital with full SEC registration).
U.S.-listed ADRs settle T+1 (aligned with the SEC settlement rule effective 5/28/2024).
mnemonics: ADR risks: 'CPT' — Currency, Political, Tax (foreign withholding).

sections.title: 7. Convertible Securities
sections.overview: Convertible securities (convertible preferred stock or convertible bonds) allow the holder to exchange the security for a fixed number of the issuer's common shares. They blend fixed-income characteristics with equity upside.
key_concepts: Conversion ratio = par / conversion price (fixed at issuance).
Parity: market prices of the convertible and the underlying common are equivalent on a converted basis.
Forced conversion: callable convertibles may be called by the issuer to compel conversion when stock price is above call value.
Holders accept a lower coupon/dividend in exchange for the conversion option.
Anti-dilution provisions adjust the conversion ratio for stock splits and stock dividends.
rules: 17 CFR 240.3a11-1 — securities convertible into stock are equity securities.
formulas: Conversion Ratio = Par Value / Conversion Price
Parity Price of Common = Market Price of Convertible / Conversion Ratio
Parity Price of Convertible = Market Price of Common × Conversion Ratio

sections.title: 8. Control and Restricted Securities — Rule 144
sections.overview: SEC Rule 144 provides a safe harbor for the public resale of restricted securities (acquired in unregistered transactions) and securities sold by control persons (affiliates). It conditions resale on holding period, volume limits, current public information, manner of sale, and filing.
key_concepts: Restricted securities: acquired in unregistered/private transactions (e.g., Reg D private placement, employee stock).
Control securities: held by an affiliate (officer, director, >10% shareholder) regardless of how acquired.
Holding period: 6 months for restricted securities of a reporting issuer; 1 year for non-reporting issuer. No holding period for control (non-restricted) securities.
Volume limit (affiliates): every 90 days, may sell the greater of 1% of outstanding shares or the average weekly trading volume over the preceding 4 weeks.
Current public information requirement on the issuer must be satisfied.
Form 144 filed with SEC if sale within 3 months exceeds 5,000 shares or $50,000 in aggregate.
Manner-of-sale requirements (brokers' transactions; no solicitation) apply to affiliates.
Non-affiliates holding restricted shares > 6 months (reporting issuer) face minimal limits; after 1 year, no Rule 144 restrictions.
rules: Resale safe harbor under SEC Rule 144 (Securities Act of 1933); citation per FINRA SIE outline 2.1.1 — 'control and restrictions (e.g., SEC Rule 144).'
formulas: Affiliate 90-day Volume Cap = max(1% of outstanding shares, average weekly trading volume over prior 4 weeks)
Form 144 Filing Trigger = sales within 3 months exceed 5,000 shares OR $50,000
mnemonics: Rule 144 conditions: 'H-V-C-M-F' — Holding period, Volume limit, Current info, Manner of sale, Form 144.

sections.title: 9. Corporate Actions
sections.overview: Corporate actions are events initiated by the issuer that affect its equity securities. They include cash and stock dividends, splits, tender offers, rights offerings, and mergers — each with mechanical price/share-count effects that must be applied to outstanding orders and option contracts.
key_concepts: Cash dividend: reduces retained earnings and cash; ex-date price drops by approximately the dividend amount.
Stock dividend / forward split: increases share count, proportionally reduces price; total ownership value unchanged.
Reverse split: reduces share count, proportionally increases price (often used to maintain listing standards).
Tender offer: a public offer to buy shares at a stated price, typically above market, often subject to minimum/maximum tender conditions.
Spin-off / split-off: distribution of a subsidiary's shares to existing shareholders.
Mergers/acquisitions: shareholders may receive cash, stock, or a combination.
Under T+1 settlement (effective 5/28/2024), the ex-dividend date and record date generally coincide (i.e., set as the same business day).
rules: 17 CFR 240.10b-18 — issuer repurchase safe harbor (a form of corporate action affecting equity).
formulas: Adjusted Price after Forward Split = Pre-Split Price × (old shares / new shares)
Adjusted Share Count = Pre-Split Shares × (new ratio / old ratio)
Ex-Dividend Price ≈ Cum-Dividend Price − Dividend per Share
mnemonics: Dividend timeline 'DERP': Declaration → Ex → Record → Payable (with Ex = Record under T+1).

sections.title: 10. Equity Issuance Concepts and Market Structure
sections.overview: Equity securities reach investors through primary offerings (IPOs and follow-ons under the Securities Act of 1933) and then trade in secondary markets governed by the Exchange Act of 1934. Issuers may also repurchase their own shares subject to a manipulation safe harbor.
key_concepts: Primary market: capital flows from investors to issuer (IPO, follow-on, rights offering).
Secondary market: trading among investors on exchanges or OTC; no proceeds to issuer.
Issuer share repurchases ('buybacks') may be conducted under a Rule 10b-18 safe harbor limiting manner, timing, price, and daily volume to avoid manipulation liability.
Voting/proxy: solicitation of proxies for shareholder meetings is regulated under Exchange Act §14.
Disclosure of control relationship: a broker-dealer controlled by, controlling, or under common control with the issuer must disclose this to customers before transactions in that security.
rules: Rule 2262 — FINRA requirement that members disclose any control relationship with the issuer of a security before entering into a customer transaction in that security; written confirmation if not initially in writing.
Rule 2261 — member must make its most recent balance sheet available to bona fide regular customers upon request.
mnemonics: 10b-18 safe harbor pillars: 'MTPV' — Manner (single broker), Timing, Price, Volume.
